concept.name: Common stock
concept.definition: A security representing a share of ownership in a company. Common stock entitles its owners to vote at shareholder meetings and to receive dividends when declared, and it represents the residual claim on the company's assets after creditors and preferred stockholders.
concept.intuition: Common stock is the basic unit of company ownership: you get a vote, a shot at dividends, and whatever value is left after everyone with a senior claim has been paid.
concept.mechanics: Companies issue common stock to raise capital, and the shares trade on exchanges or over the counter. Returns come from price appreciation and dividends, both uncertain; in a liquidation, bondholders are paid first, then preferred stockholders, and common stockholders receive whatever remains, which may be nothing.
concept.failure_modes: Common stockholders are last in line in bankruptcy and can lose the entire investment. Prices fluctuate with company-specific and market-wide events, and issuance of new shares can dilute existing holders.
concept.misconceptions: That dividends on common stock are guaranteed — the board can raise, cut, or omit them at its discretion. Also, owning shares does not give a claim on any specific corporate asset.
concept.example: Buying 200 shares of a listed company gives the investor 200 votes at the annual meeting and any per-share dividend the board declares.
